claims.claim: The amplitude and total charge transfer of ISC events were smaller in cochleae in P2ry1 KO mice relative to controls.
claims.source: Consistent with the involvement of P2RY1, the amplitude and total charge transfer of ISC events (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B) and size of spontaneous crenations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D) were smaller in cochleae in P2ry1 KO mice relative to controls.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The size of spontaneous crenations was smaller in cochleae in P2ry1 KO mice relative to controls.
claims.source: Consistent with the involvement of P2RY1, the amplitude and total charge transfer of ISC events (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B) and size of spontaneous crenations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D) were smaller in cochleae in P2ry1 KO mice relative to controls.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Supporting cells in P2ry1 KO mice exhibited more frequent, small amplitude currents that were not blocked by MRS2500 or broad-spectrum P2 receptor antagonists.
claims.source: However, supporting cells in P2ry1 KO mice exhibited some aberrant, gain-of-function activity consisting of more frequent, small amplitude currents (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B), that were not blocked by MRS2500 or broad-spectrum P2 receptor antagonists (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Application of MRS2500 (1 µM) abolished spontaneous currents in IHCs.
claims.source: To assess whether P2RY1 signaling is also required for periodic excitation of IHCs prior to hearing onset, we assessed the sensitivity of spontaneous IHC inward currents to MRS2500 (Figure 3F). Consistent with the supporting cell origin of IHC activity, application of MRS2500 (1 µM) also abolished spontaneous currents in IHCs (Figure 3F,G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3F,G.

claims.claim: P2RY1 is the primary purinergic autoreceptor on ISCs responsible for inducing periodic excitation of IHCs prior to hearing onset.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that P2RY1 is the primary purinergic autoreceptor on ISCs responsible for inducing periodic excitation of IHCs prior to hearing onset.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results with MRS2500.

claims.claim: A progressively increasing inward current appeared in both ISCs and IHCs with prolonged application of MRS2500.
claims.source: Although P2RY1 inhibition abolished most transient inward currents in both ISCs and IHCs, a progressively increasing inward current (downward shift in baseline) appeared in both cell types with prolonged application of MRS2500 (Figure 3B,F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B,F.

claims.claim: The progressively increasing inward current in IHCs and ISCs following P2RY1 inhibition arises from accumulation of K+ released from cells in the organ of Corti.
claims.source: Prior studies in CNS brain slices indicated that Gq-coupled purinergic receptors in astrocytes regulate extracellular K+ concentration and neuronal excitability (Wang et al., 2012). The slowly progressing nature of the response in IHCs and ISCs suggest that it may arise from accumulation of K+ released from cells in the organ of Corti.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experiments inhibiting K+ sources.

claims.claim: When IHC and SGN excitation was inhibited with cadmium and tetrodotoxin, and K+ transporters were inhibited with ouabain and bumetanide, no inward current was induced in ISCs upon blocking P2RY1.
claims.source: Indeed, when IHC and SGN excitation was inhibited with cadmium (CdCl2, 100 µM) and tetrodotoxin (TTX, 1 µM), and K+ transporters Na,K-ATPase and NKCC were inhibited with ouabain (10 µM) and bumetanide (50 µM), no inward current was induced in ISCs upon blocking P2RY1 (Figure 3H,I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3H,I.

claims.claim: When whole cell recordings were performed from IHCs using an internal solution containing Cs+ and TEA, MRS2500 did not induce an inward current.
claims.source: Similarly, if K+ accumulation is responsible for the current in IHCs, it should be abolished when the ability of IHCs to detect changes in K+ is reduced. When whole cell recordings were performed from IHCs using an internal solution containing Cs+ and TEA, which blocks most IHC K+ channels (Kros et al., 1998; Marcotti et al., 2003), MRS2500 also did not induce an inward current (Figure 3J,K).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3J,K.

claims.claim: P2RY1 has two distinct effects in the cochlea: it induces the transient inward currents that trigger IHC burst firing and it accelerates clearance of K+ away from IHCs within the organ of Corti.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that P2RY1 has two distinct effects in the cochlea; it induces the transient inward currents that trigger IHC burst firing (Figure 3F; see also Figure 6D,G) and it accelerates clearance of K+ away from IHCs within the organ of Corti.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Focal P2RY1 stimulation with MRS2365 (10 μM) elicits an inward current and crenations in ISCs in control but not P2ry1 KO mice.
claims.source: Focal P2RY1 stimulation with a selective agonist (MRS2365, 10 μM), which mimics the effect of endogenous ATP by eliciting an inward current and crenations in ISCs in control but not P2ry1 KO mice (Figure 4A–C), was combined with assessments of the reversal potential of K+ currents in IHCs using a voltage protocol similar to that used to assess extracellular K+ buildup at vestibular calyceal synapses (Lim et al., 2011) (Figure 4D–F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A–C.

claims.claim: Following transient stimulation of P2RY1, K+ tail currents in IHCs immediately shifted inward, consistent with an increase in extracellular K+.
claims.source: Following transient stimulation of P2RY1, these K+ tail currents immediately shifted inward, as would be expected if extracellular K+ increases (Figure 4G,J), consistent with the effects metabotropic purinergic receptor stimulation on synaptically-evoked K+ currents in IHCs (Wang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4G,J.

claims.claim: After a few seconds following P2RY1 stimulation, K+ tail currents in IHCs shifted outward relative to baseline, indicative of a gradual decrease in extracellular K+ below that present prior to P2RY1 stimulation.
claims.source: However, after a few seconds these K+ currents shifted outward relative to baseline, indicative of a gradual decrease in extracellular K+ below that present prior to P2RY1 stimulation, before gradually returning to pre-stimulation levels after several minutes (Figure 4G,J).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4G,J.

claims.claim: The outward shift in K+ tail current closely followed the time course of supporting cell crenation.
claims.source: The outward shift in K+ tail current closely followed the time course of supporting cell crenation (Figure 4G), suggesting that the shrinkage of ISCs induced by P2RY1 activation results in a prolonged increase in extracellular space around IHCs that allows greater dilution and more rapid redistribution of K+ in the organ of Corti.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The shrinkage of ISCs induced by P2RY1 activation results in a prolonged increase in extracellular space around IHCs that allows greater dilution and more rapid redistribution of K+ in the organ of Corti.
claims.source: The outward shift in K+ tail current closely followed the time course of supporting cell crenation (Figure 4G), suggesting that the shrinkage of ISCs induced by P2RY1 activation results in a prolonged increase in extracellular space around IHCs that allows greater dilution and more rapid redistribution of K+ in the organ of Corti.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal correlation between crenation and K+ tail current changes.

claims.claim: Focal application of KCl (130 mM) into the supporting cell syncytium near IHCs in the presence of P2RY1 antagonists induced an inward shift in K+ tail currents but they rapidly returned to baseline and did not shift outward.
claims.source: To determine if rapid increases in extracellular K+ and Cl– were sufficient to stimulate K+ redistribution in the absence of crenation, we focally applied KCl (130 mM) into the supporting cell syncytium near IHCs in the presence of P2RY1 antagonists (Figure 4H,J). As expected, this transient increase in extracellular K+ induced an inward shift in K+ tail currents and a brief optical change induced by fluid delivery; however, K+ tail currents rapidly returned to baseline and did not shift outward, suggesting that extracellular K+ (and Cl–) elevation are not sufficient to enhance K+ redistribution rates.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4H,J.

claims.claim: Extracellular K+ (and Cl–) elevation are not sufficient to enhance K+ redistribution rates in the absence of crenation.
claims.source: To determine if rapid increases in extracellular K+ and Cl– were sufficient to stimulate K+ redistribution in the absence of crenation, we focally applied KCl (130 mM) into the supporting cell syncytium near IHCs in the presence of P2RY1 antagonists (Figure 4H,J). As expected, this transient increase in extracellular K+ induced an inward shift in K+ tail currents and a brief optical change induced by fluid delivery; however, K+ tail currents rapidly returned to baseline and did not shift outward, suggesting that extracellular K+ (and Cl–) elevation are not sufficient to enhance K+ redistribution rates.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the KCl puff experiment.

claims.claim: In Tecta-Cre;TMEM16Afl/fl mice, ISCs failed to crenate, IHCs did not depolarize, and K+ tail currents remained stable following P2RY1 stimulation.
claims.source: In addition, we transiently stimulated P2RY1 in Tecta-Cre;TMEM16Afl/fl mice, in which purinergic receptor activation is preserved, but crenations are abolished (Wang et al., 2015). In these mice, ISCs failed to crenate, IHCs did not depolarize, and K+ tail currents remained stable throughout the duration of the recording (Figure 4I,J).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4I,J.

claims.claim: Purinergic autoreceptors on ISCs influence extracellular K+ levels by triggering K+ release and by altering K+ redistribution by controlling the size of the extracellular space.
claims.source: These results suggest that purinergic autoreceptors on ISCs influence extracellular K+ levels by triggering K+ release and by altering K+ redistribution by controlling the size of the extracellular space.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results with MRS2365, KCl puffs, and TMEM16A knockout mice.

claims.claim: Spontaneous Ca2+ elevations that occur simultaneously within groups of ISCs, IHCs, and SGNs were abolished following inhibition of P2RY1 with MRS2500.
claims.source: Time lapse imaging revealed that the spontaneous Ca2+ elevations that occur simultaneously within groups of ISCs, IHCs, and SGNs (Eckrich et al., 2018; Tritsch and Bergles, 2010; Zhang-Hooks et al., 2016) (Figure 5A) were abolished following inhibition of P2RY1 with MRS2500 (Figure 5B,C) and were dramatically reduced in P2ry1 KO mice (Pax2-Cre;R26-lsl-GCaMP3;P2ry1–/–) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Spontaneous Ca2+ elevations that occur simultaneously within groups of ISCs, IHCs, and SGNs were dramatically reduced in P2ry1 KO mice.
claims.source: Time lapse imaging revealed that the spontaneous Ca2+ elevations that occur simultaneously within groups of ISCs, IHCs, and SGNs (Eckrich et al., 2018; Tritsch and Bergles, 2010; Zhang-Hooks et al., 2016) (Figure 5A) were abolished following inhibition of P2RY1 with MRS2500 (Figure 5B,C) and were dramatically reduced in P2ry1 KO mice (Pax2-Cre;R26-lsl-GCaMP3;P2ry1–/–) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There was a gradual increase in spontaneous, uncoordinated Ca2+ transients in IHCs in the presence of MRS2500.
claims.source: Moreover, in accordance with the progressive increase in extracellular K+ that follows P2RY1 inhibition, there was a gradual increase in spontaneous, uncoordinated Ca2+ transients in IHCs in the presence of MRS2500 (Figure 5D–F), suggesting that this K+ accumulation increases IHC firing.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D–F.

claims.claim: IHCs in P2ry1 KO mice displayed a higher level of uncorrelated Ca2+ transients.
claims.source: Similarly, IHCs in P2ry1 KO mice displayed a higher level of uncorrelated Ca2+ transients in hair cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E), indicative of enhanced excitability.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: P2RY1 is required for coordinated activation of ISCs, IHCs, and SGNs before hearing onset.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that P2RY1 is required for coordinated activation of ISCs, IHCs, and SGNs before hearing onset and that P2RY1 inhibition leads to higher rates of uncorrelated activity.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the calcium imaging results.

claims.claim: P2RY1 inhibition leads to higher rates of uncorrelated activity in IHCs.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that P2RY1 is required for coordinated activation of ISCs, IHCs, and SGNs before hearing onset and that P2RY1 inhibition leads to higher rates of uncorrelated activity.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the calcium imaging results.

claims.claim: Application of MRS2500 resulted in a dramatic reduction of high frequency burst firing in SGNs.
claims.source: To determine if P2RY1 initiates burst firing in SGNs, we recorded spontaneous activity from SGNs using juxtacellular recordings from their somata (Figure 6A). Application of MRS2500 resulted in a dramatic reduction of high frequency burst firing in SGNs, visible as a decrease in burst frequency and action potentials per burst (Figure 6E,F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: All SGN spiking was abolished by the AMPA receptor antagonist NBQX (50 µM).
claims.source: All SGN spiking was abolished by the AMPA receptor antagonist NBQX (50 µM) (Figure 6D), indicating that their activity requires synaptic excitation by IHCs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: SGN activity requires synaptic excitation by IHCs.
claims.source: All SGN spiking was abolished by the AMPA receptor antagonist NBQX (50 µM) (Figure 6D), indicating that their activity requires synaptic excitation by IHCs.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the NBQX experiment.

claims.claim: The precise patterning of action potentials within bursts was disrupted by P2RY1 inhibition, with fewer interspike intervals in the 75–125 ms range.
claims.source: The precise patterning of action potentials within bursts was also disrupted by P2RY1 inhibition, as there were fewer interspike intervals in the 75–125 ms range (Figure 6C,F), which correspond to the maximum rate of Ca2+ spike generation by IHCs during ATP-mediated excitation (Tritsch et al., 2010b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C,F.

claims.claim: The coefficient of variation measured for interspike intervals was significantly lower following P2RY1 inhibition, suggesting SGNs fire more randomly.
claims.source: Additionally, the coefficient of variation measured for interspike intervals was significantly lower following P2RY1 inhibition, suggesting SGNs fire more randomly (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The average frequency of action potentials in SGNs remained unchanged during P2RY1 inhibition due to increases in non-burst firing.
claims.source: However, the average frequency of action potentials remained unchanged during P2RY1 inhibition (Figure 6E) due to increases in non-burst firing, consistent with depolarizing inward currents observed in IHCs with P2RY1 inhibition (Figure 3F,K).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: SGNs in P2ry1 KO cochleae exhibited a lower burst firing rate, fewer interspike intervals in the 75–125 ms range, and a lower coefficient of variation of interspike intervals relative to controls.
claims.source: SGNs in P2ry1 KO cochleae exhibited activity similar to wildtype SGNs in the presence of MRS2500, with a lower burst firing rate, fewer interspike intervals in the 75–125 ms range, and a lower coefficient of variation of interspike intervals relative to controls (Figure 6G–I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6G–I.

claims.claim: Some burst-like behavior was still observed in SGNs in P2ry1 KO mice, suggesting that other forms of excitation emerge in the absence of P2RY1.
claims.source: However, despite the profound contribution of P2RY1 to ISC and IHC activity, some burst-like behavior (clustered, but lacking the same density of action potentials in control conditions) was still observed in SGNs (Figure 6C,D,G) suggesting that other forms of excitation emerge in the absence of P2RY1, perhaps due to the increase in overall excitability or compensatory developmental changes.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: P2RY1 is required to generate discrete bursts of action potentials in SGNs.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that P2RY1 is required to generate discrete bursts of action potentials in SGNs and that loss of these receptors enhances uncorrelated firing.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the SGN recording results.

claims.claim: Loss of P2RY1 enhances uncorrelated firing in SGNs.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that P2RY1 is required to generate discrete bursts of action potentials in SGNs and that loss of these receptors enhances uncorrelated firing.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the SGN recording results.

claims.claim: Both control and P2ry1 KO mice exhibited correlated neuronal activity confined to stationary bands oriented along the tonotopic axis in the inferior colliculus.

claims.claim: Events in the inferior colliculus of P2ry1 KO mice were similar in amplitude and duration (half-width) to controls.
claims.source: Spontaneous events were less frequent in P2ry1 KO mice (9.7 ± 0.8 events per minute compared to 13.4 ± 0.7 events per minute in control; two-tailed Student's t test, p=0.002), although the events were similar in amplitude and duration (half-width) (Figure 7D), suggesting that some compensatory amplification of events occurs in these mice.

claims.claim: Some compensatory amplification of events occurs in P2ry1 KO mice.
claims.source: Spontaneous events were less frequent in P2ry1 KO mice (9.7 ± 0.8 events per minute compared to 13.4 ± 0.7 events per minute in control; two-tailed Student's t test, p=0.002), although the events were similar in amplitude and duration (half-width) (Figure 7D), suggesting that some compensatory amplification of events occurs in these mice.

claims.claim: The contralateral bias exhibited for each event in the inferior colliculus was higher in P2ry1 KO mice, with the weaker relative to stronger side amplitude decreasing from 0.61 ± 0.02 to 0.44 ± 0.02.
claims.source: First, the contralateral bias exhibited for each event was higher, with the weaker relative to stronger side amplitude decreasing from 0.61 ± 0.02 to 0.44 ± 0.02 (two-tailed Student's t test, p=3.0e-6) (Figure 7D).

claims.claim: The coefficient of variation of event amplitudes in the inferior colliculus was 40% higher in P2ry1 KO mice relative to controls.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Activity in brain areas later responsible for processing higher frequency tones (~8–16 kHz) exhibited the greatest reduction (68%) in P2ry1 KO mice, while activity in low frequency areas was unaltered.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7E–H.

claims.claim: In P2ry1 KO mice, bilateral removal of both cochleae abolished activity in the inferior colliculus.
claims.source: In P2ry1 KO mice, bilateral removal of both cochleae abolished activity in the IC, demonstrating that activity in these mice still originates in the periphery (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).

claims.claim: Activity in P2ry1 KO mice still originates in the periphery.

claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the cochlear ablation experiment.

claims.claim: Intense periods of neuronal activity dramatically alter the ionic composition of the extracellular environment, leaving behind excess K+ that can alter neuronal excitability.
claims.source: Intense periods of neuronal activity dramatically alter the ionic composition of the extracellular environment, leaving behind excess K+ that can alter neuronal excitability, induce spontaneous activity and trigger debilitating seizures.

claims.source: Indeed, infusion of ATP into the inner ear profoundly reduces sound-evoked compound action potentials in the auditory nerve (Bobbin and Thompson, 1978; Muñoz et al., 1995), presumably due to decreased endolymphatic potential following shunting inhibition through P2RX2 (Housley et al., 2013) or excitotoxic damage (Cisneros-Mejorado et al., 2015) to IHCs or SGNs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claims.claim: P2RX2 null mice and humans with a P2RX2 variant (c.178G > T) experience progressive sensorineural hearing loss.
claims.source: Consistent with these observations, P2RX2 null mice and humans with a P2RX2 variant (c.178G > T) experience progressive sensorineural hearing loss (Yan et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

results.result: Spontaneous activity in inner supporting cells (ISCs) requires Ca2+ release from intracellular stores via a Gq-coupled purinergic receptor and PLC signaling pathway, but not ryanodine receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 demonstrate that BAPTA-AM and thapsigargin abolish spontaneous ISC currents and crenations (Figure 1), establishing the necessity of intracellular Ca2+ stores. Claim C59 shows ryanodine has no effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), ruling out ryanodine receptors. The PLC inhibitor U73122 (but not inactive analog U73343) reduced activity, supporting C60's conclusion about Gq-coupled receptor/PLC signaling. The experimental controls are appropriate and the logic is sound.

results.result: P2RY1 is highly expressed in inner supporting cells of the developing cochlea, with expression levels >100-fold higher than other P2RY receptors and increasing during early postnatal development concurrent with spontaneous activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are supported by gene expression data (Figure 2A) showing P2RY1 dominance and developmental increase. Claims C63-C64 are supported by X-gal staining in P2ry1-LacZ reporter mice (Figure 2B-C) showing ISC-specific expression. The localization and expression data converge to support P2RY1 as the candidate receptor. However, the gene expression data relies on a citation (Scheffer et al., 2015) rather than original data.

results.result: P2RY1 is the primary purinergic autoreceptor responsible for spontaneous activity in ISCs and IHCs, as demonstrated by pharmacological inhibition with MRS2500 and genetic deletion in P2ry1 KO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 show MRS2500 markedly reduces ISC currents and crenations at both room and physiological temperature (Figure 3B-E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Claims C67-C68 show reduced amplitude and crenation size in P2ry1 KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). Claim C70 demonstrates MRS2500 abolishes IHC spontaneous currents (Figure 3F-G). The convergence of pharmacological and genetic evidence strongly supports C71's conclusion. Claim C69 notes aberrant activity in KO mice not blocked by antagonists, suggesting compensatory changes.

results.result: P2RY1 inhibition causes progressive K+ accumulation in the extracellular space, leading to inward currents in both ISCs and IHCs, demonstrating a dual role for P2RY1 in both triggering K+ release and accelerating K+ clearance.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 documents the progressive inward current following MRS2500 (Figure 3B,F). Claims C74-C75 provide strong mechanistic evidence: blocking K+ sources (CdCl2, TTX, ouabain, bumetanide) prevents the inward current in ISCs (Figure 3H-I), and blocking IHC K+ channels (Cs+/TEA internal) prevents the inward current in IHCs (Figure 3J-K). This supports C73's interpretation of K+ accumulation. Claim C76's conclusion about P2RY1's dual role is well-supported by the convergent evidence.

results.result: P2RY1 activation increases extracellular space through ISC crenation, which enhances K+ clearance from the extracellular environment around IHCs, as demonstrated by K+ tail current measurements and control experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 show that P2RY1 stimulation with MRS2365 causes initial inward shift (K+ increase) followed by outward shift (K+ decrease below baseline) in IHC K+ tail currents (Figure 4A-C, G, J). Claim C80 shows the outward shift correlates temporally with crenation. Claims C82-C83 show KCl puffs without crenation do not produce the outward shift (Figure 4H,J), demonstrating crenation is necessary. Claim C84 shows no K+ clearance enhancement in TMEM16A knockout mice that cannot crenate (Figure 4I,J). The convergent evidence from agonist stimulation, control experiments, and genetic manipulation strongly supports C85's conclusion.

results.result: P2RY1 is required for coordinated Ca2+ activity among ISCs, IHCs, and SGNs, and its inhibition leads to increased uncorrelated activity in IHCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 show coordinated Ca2+ transients are abolished by MRS2500 and dramatically reduced in P2ry1 KO mice (Figure 5A-C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B). Claims C88-C89 show increased uncorrelated IHC Ca2+ transients following P2RY1 inhibition (Figure 5D-F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E). The calcium imaging data clearly demonstrates both loss of coordination and gain of uncorrelated activity, supporting claims C90-C91. The use of correlation analysis (correlation matrices) provides quantitative support.

results.result: P2RY1 is required for discrete burst firing in spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), with inhibition reducing burst frequency and disrupting interspike interval patterns while maintaining overall firing frequency through increased tonic firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C92, C95-C97 show MRS2500 reduces burst firing, disrupts interspike intervals (fewer 75-125 ms intervals), lowers coefficient of variation, but maintains average firing frequency (Figure 6B-F). Claims C93-C94 show NBQX abolishes all SGN activity, confirming IHC synaptic drive (Figure 6D). Claim C98 shows similar phenotype in P2ry1 KO mice (Figure 6G-I). Claim C99 notes residual burst-like activity in KO mice, suggesting compensatory mechanisms. The juxtacellular recording data strongly supports claims C100-C101 about P2RY1's role in burst generation and the enhancement of uncorrelated firing upon its loss.

results.result: P2ry1 KO mice show reduced frequency but preserved spatial organization of spontaneous activity in the inferior colliculus, with frequency-specific deficits in high-frequency processing regions and evidence of compensatory amplification.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 show P2ry1 KO mice have reduced event frequency (9.7 vs 13.4 events/min) but similar amplitude and duration (Figure 7A-D). Claims C106-C107 show increased contralateral bias and 40% higher coefficient of variation in KO mice (Figure 7D). Claim C108 shows 68% reduction in high-frequency zones but no change in low-frequency areas (Figure 7E-H). Claims C109-C110 show bilateral cochlear ablation abolishes IC activity in KO mice, confirming peripheral origin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The in vivo imaging data supports these claims, though C105's interpretation of "compensatory amplification" is speculative given only preserved amplitude.

results.result: Acute systemic inhibition of P2RY1 with MRS2500 dramatically reduces spontaneous activity in the inferior colliculus without affecting superior colliculus retinal waves, demonstrating P2RY1's critical role in cochlea-generated auditory activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 show MRS2500 injection reduces IC event frequency (13.3 to 3.9 events/min) and amplitude within 5 minutes (Figure 8A-D). Claim C113 shows SC retinal wave activity is unaffected (Figure 8B,C,E), demonstrating specificity. Claim C115 shows inhibition occurs evenly across tonotopic regions, unlike the frequency-specific deficit in KO mice (Figure 8F,G). The acute pharmacological manipulation provides strong evidence for C116's conclusion about P2RY1's critical role. Claim C114's interpretation about cochlear locus is reasonable given the blood-tissue barrier permeability at this age.

results.result: P2RY1 autoreceptors in inner supporting cells control hair cell burst firing through a dual mechanism: triggering K+ efflux/depolarization and controlling extracellular space volume to regulate K+ redistribution, with inhibition causing K+ accumulation and tonic firing.
results.evaluation: These abstract claims synthesize the major findings. Claims C1-C6 describe P2RY1's role in triggering burst firing through K+ efflux, depolarization, and crenation-mediated extracellular space expansion. Claims C7-C11 describe the unexpected finding that P2RY1 inhibition enhances tonic firing through reduced extracellular space and K+ accumulation. Claim C12 provides the overarching conclusion. All claims are supported by the detailed experimental evidence in the Results section, making this a well-supported synthesis of the manuscript's main findings.

results.result: P2RY1 autoreceptors in ISCs are the key initial step in generating spontaneous activity in the auditory system, inducing Ca2+ release that opens TMEM16A channels, with both pharmacological and genetic evidence showing dramatic reduction in burst firing and coordinated activation.
results.evaluation: These introduction claims summarize the main findings that are subsequently demonstrated in the Results section. Claims C44-C45 identify P2RY1 as the key receptor and its mechanism. Claims C46-C48 state the effects of inhibition/deletion on burst firing and coordination. Claims C49-C51 describe the unexpected finding about K+ clearance and tonic firing. Claim C52 mentions the in vivo evidence. Claim C53 provides the overall conclusion. All these claims are supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

results.result: P2RY1 activation has a dual function in the developing auditory system: triggering episodic K+-dependent depolarization of hair cells and enhancing K+ clearance by increasing extracellular space volume, promoting discrete bursts of activity.
results.evaluation: These Discussion claims synthesize the main findings. Claim C123 identifies P2RY1 as a Gq-coupled metabotropic receptor initiating spontaneous activity. Claims C124-C125 summarize the effects of P2RY1 manipulation on spontaneous activity and K+ clearance. Claim C126 articulates the "duality of purpose" concept. All claims are well-supported by the experimental data presented in the Results section and represent appropriate synthesis of the findings.

results.result: P2RY1 is both necessary and sufficient for spontaneous current generation in supporting cells, and acute in vivo inhibition profoundly decreases cochlea-generated activity in the auditory midbrain.
results.evaluation: Claim C136 states P2RY1 is necessary and sufficient based on pharmacological studies (Figures 3B and 4B). Claim C137 states acute in vivo inhibition decreases midbrain activity (Figure 8C). Both claims are directly supported by experimental data. The "necessary and sufficient" language in C136 is justified by the near-complete abolition of activity with MRS2500 and the ability of the agonist MRS2365 to trigger activity.

results.result: P2RY1 controls extracellular space volume in the organ of Corti through osmotic shrinkage/swelling of ISCs, with activation increasing space and enhancing K+ dissipation, while inhibition decreases space leading to K+ accumulation and IHC depolarization.
results.evaluation: These Discussion claims synthesize the extracellular space findings. Claims C141-C144 describe the effects of P2RY1 activation on ISC crenation and K+ dissipation. Claims C145-C146 describe the effects of P2RY1 inhibition on ISC swelling and K+ accumulation. Claim C147 notes consistency with TMEM16A cKO mice. All claims are well-supported by the experimental data in Figures 3-4 and represent appropriate interpretation of the findings.

results.result: Basal P2RY1 activation hyperpolarizes IHCs by expanding extracellular space and lowering K+ concentrations, increasing their dynamic range and enabling finer control of excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C150 propose that basal P2RY1 activation sets a hyperpolarized baseline for IHCs. While this interpretation is consistent with the observation that P2RY1 inhibition causes depolarization and K+ accumulation, the manuscript does not directly measure basal P2RY1 activity levels or demonstrate that tonic receptor activation maintains a hyperpolarized state. This is a reasonable inference but lacks direct experimental support.

results.result: K+ redistribution mechanisms in ISCs are weak at this developmental stage, as evidenced by the abolition of tonic inward currents when K+ release pathways are inhibited and the high input resistance of uncoupled ISCs suggesting few K+ leak channels.
results.evaluation: Claim C151 shows the tonic inward current is abolished when K+ release pathways are inhibited (Figure 3H,I), supporting C152's interpretation of weak K+ redistribution. Claims C153-C155 cite prior work showing ISCs have membrane potential close to EK but high input resistance when uncoupled, supporting C156's inference of few K+ leak channels. The logic is sound and the cited evidence is appropriate.

results.result: Astrocytes and cochlear ISCs use purinergic signaling in distinct ways to control extracellular K+ and neuronal excitability, with astrocytes using Na,K-ATPase activation while ISCs use extracellular space volume changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C163 describe astrocyte K+ buffering mechanisms from the literature. Claims C164-C165 note that while P2RY1 is expressed in astrocytes, the astrocyte mechanism does not appear to operate in the cochlea based on TMEM16A cKO experiments (Figure 4I,J). Claim C166 synthesizes these findings to conclude distinct mechanisms. The comparison is well-supported by the experimental data and literature, though the conclusion relies on the assumption that TMEM16A cKO mice have intact metabotropic signaling.

results.result: Systemic P2RY1 inhibitor infusion specifically decreases inferior colliculus activity while sparing superior colliculus retinal waves, indicating the locus of action is in the cochlea rather than CNS astrocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C169 show MRS2500 decreases IC activity but not SC retinal waves (Figure 8). Claim C170 notes that astrocyte P2RY1 inhibition would enhance rather than inhibit neuronal activity. The specificity of the effect and the logic about astrocyte function support the interpretation that the drug acts in the cochlea. However, the manuscript acknowledges (C173) that some CNS effects are possible, introducing some uncertainty.

results.result: Developing sensory systems exhibit robust homeostatic mechanisms that preserve spontaneous activity despite disruption of key components, as evidenced by persistent activity in P2ry1 KO mice in low-frequency IC regions, likely due to compensatory developmental changes.
results.evaluation: Claim C175 notes persistent activity in central IC regions of P2ry1 KO mice (low-frequency processing areas). Claims C176 and C182 propose compensatory changes as an explanation. Claim C177 states this is a general principle in developing sensory systems. While the observation of persistent activity is supported by data (Figure 7), the interpretation of "compensatory changes" is speculative. The manuscript does not identify specific compensatory mechanisms or demonstrate that they are responsible for the preserved activity.

results.result: Neurons in developing sensory pathways exhibit spontaneous bursts of electrical activity critical for survival, maturation, and circuit refinement, with activity arising within sensory organs, but mechanisms in the cochlea remain poorly understood compared to the retina.
results.evaluation: These introduction claims establish the background and motivation for the study. Claims C13-C14 state general principles about spontaneous activity in development. Claims C15-C16 identify the knowledge gap regarding cochlear mechanisms. Claims C17-C26 provide context about neuronal development and spontaneous activity. All claims are appropriately supported by citations to prior literature and represent accurate statements of the field's knowledge.

results.result: One model proposes cholinergic efferents initiate burst firing through intermittent hyperpolarization of IHCs, but evidence from knockout mice and in vitro studies suggests efferents modulate temporal characteristics rather than being essential for burst initiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 describe the cholinergic efferent model with appropriate citations. Claims C29-C32 present evidence that challenges this model: burst firing persists in α9 receptor KO mice and in vitro without efferents. Claim C33 provides the interpretation that efferents modulate but are not essential. This is an accurate summary of prior work that motivates the alternative model explored in the manuscript.

results.result: An alternative model proposes IHCs fire bursts due to K+ release from inner supporting cells following ATP release and purinergic receptor activation, leading to Ca2+ increase, TMEM16A channel opening, and ion/water efflux causing ISC shrinkage.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 introduce the alternative model and anatomical context. Claims C37-C41 describe the signaling cascade from ATP release through K+ efflux and ISC crenation. All claims are appropriately supported by citations to prior literature and accurately represent the existing model that the manuscript builds upon and extends.

results.result: The molecular identity of purinergic receptors involved in cochlear spontaneous activity has remained elusive, and few in vivo manipulations have been performed, limiting understanding of how cochlear activity influences central auditory circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 establish key knowledge gaps that motivate the study: the unknown receptor identity and lack of in vivo manipulations. These statements accurately represent the state of the field prior to this work and provide clear justification for the experimental approach taken in the manuscript.

results.result: Intense neuronal activity alters extracellular ionic composition, with glial cells controlling K+ homeostasis in the CNS through passive and active mechanisms, while less is known about peripheral nervous system mechanisms, though cochlear supporting cells are thought to redistribute K+.
results.evaluation: These Discussion claims provide context for the findings. Claims C117-C119 describe general principles of K+ homeostasis and glial function in the CNS. Claim C120 identifies a knowledge gap in the peripheral nervous system. Claims C121-C122 describe the role of cochlear supporting cells. All claims represent accurate statements of established knowledge and appropriately frame the significance of the findings.

results.result: The mechanism of ATP release from ISCs remains undefined but may involve gap-junction hemichannels, as gap-junction antagonists inhibit spontaneous activity and lowering extracellular calcium enhances activity frequency.
results.evaluation: Claim C127 acknowledges the undefined mechanism. Claim C128 proposes gap-junction hemichannels as a hypothesis. Claims C129-C130 cite evidence supporting this hypothesis. While the cited evidence is consistent with the hypothesis, the manuscript does not directly test the ATP release mechanism. This represents a reasonable speculation based on prior work but lacks direct experimental support in the current study.

results.result: ATP activates ISC purinergic receptors triggering Ca2+ increase, TMEM16A opening, and Cl-/K+ efflux, which depolarizes IHCs causing Ca2+ action potentials and glutamate release that activates SGNs, with bursts propagating through the auditory system and likely activating olivocochlear efferents.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C133 describe the established signaling cascade from ATP to SGN activation, appropriately supported by citations. Claim C134 states bursts propagate through the auditory system with citation support. Claim C135 proposes olivocochlear efferent activation as a hypothesis. Most claims are well-supported by prior literature, though C135 is speculative ("likely," "may modulate").

results.result: The reliance on P2RY1 is unexpected given widespread expression of other purinergic receptors in the cochlea, possibly reflecting spatial-temporal characteristics of ATP release or involvement of other nucleotides like ADP.
results.evaluation: Claim C138 notes the unexpected specificity for P2RY1 given expression of other receptors. Claims C139-C140 propose hypotheses for this specificity: spatial-temporal ATP release characteristics or involvement of ADP. While these are reasonable hypotheses supported by citations about nucleotidase activity, the manuscript does not directly test these mechanisms. This represents informed speculation rather than demonstrated findings.

results.result: Tight junctions and limited K+ conductance of ISCs may restrict passive K+ diffusion in the cochlea, necessitating uptake via K+-Cl- symporters, Na,K-ATPase, and inwardly-rectifying K+ channels, though the apparently low capacity of these systems increases dependence on extracellular volume-mediated diffusion.
results.evaluation: Claim C157 proposes that anatomical features restrict K+ diffusion, supported by a citation to vestibular epithelium. Claim C158 describes expression of K+ uptake systems. Claim C159 interprets the findings as indicating low capacity of these systems. While C158 represents established knowledge, claims C157 and C159 are interpretations not directly tested in the manuscript. The inference about "low capacity" is based on the K+ accumulation observed with P2RY1 inhibition, but alternative explanations are possible.

results.result: The blood-labyrinth barrier in the inner ear is not fully formed prior to hearing onset, permitting pharmacological access to the cochlea at this developmental stage.
results.evaluation: Claim C167 is supported by citation to Suzuki et al. (1998) and is used to justify the in vivo pharmacological experiments. This is an appropriate use of prior literature to support the experimental design.

results.result: P2ry1 mRNA is expressed in the cochlear nucleus and can mediate calcium transients in spherical bushy cells, raising the possibility that some effects of MRS2500 result from CNS actions.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C172 cite prior work showing P2RY1 expression and function in the cochlear nucleus. Claim C173 speculates that some MRS2500 effects might result from CNS actions. While this is a reasonable caveat, the manuscript's data showing specificity to IC (not SC) and the logic about astrocyte function argue against major CNS contributions. This represents appropriate acknowledgment of uncertainty rather than a demonstrated finding.

results.result: Developing sensory systems show robust homeostatic mechanisms preserving spontaneous activity despite disruption of key components, as seen in visual and auditory systems, with P2ry1 KO mice potentially engaging other purinergic receptors or showing compensatory changes in central circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C181 cite examples from visual and auditory systems showing preserved activity despite genetic disruptions. Claim C182 interprets this as robust homeostatic mechanisms. Claims C183-C185 speculate about mechanisms in P2ry1 KO mice. While the cited examples are accurate, the proposed mechanisms for P2ry1 KO mice (other receptors, compensatory changes) are speculative and not directly tested.

results.result: Preservation of early patterned activity in children with deafness mutations may improve outcomes of later therapeutic interventions to restore hearing.
results.evaluation: Claim C186 speculates about clinical implications of homeostatic preservation of activity. While this is a reasonable hypothesis, it is entirely speculative and not tested in the manuscript. This represents a potential future direction rather than a supported finding.

results.result: Purinergic receptors are widely expressed in the adult inner ear and may serve neuroprotective roles, with ATP infusion reducing auditory nerve responses and P2RX2 variants causing hearing loss, while metabotropic receptors may contribute to K+ buffering after noise damage or IHC gain control.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C193 cite prior work on purinergic receptor expression and function in the adult cochlea. Claims C189, C194, and C195 propose hypotheses about neuroprotective roles, K+ buffering after trauma, and gain control. While the cited literature is appropriate, the proposed functions (C194-C195) are speculative and not tested in the manuscript. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work rather than demonstrated findings.
